technology.title: Smartphone shipments face another bleak year before modest 2028 comeback
technology.description: Global smartphone shipments are forecast to fall 14 percent this year and another 6 percent in 2027, with a recovery not expected until 2028. That's the outlook from Counterpoint Research's latest Smartphone Market Outlook Tracker , which points to rising memory costs and constrained supplies as continuing pressure on handset makers and buyers. The downturn was particularly sharp in the third quarter: IDC and Omdia estimated year-on-year shipment declines of 22 percent and 20 percent respectively, as rising prices and component shortages squeezed the market. Don't expect things to get better in the short term, as Counterpoint forecasts another 6 percent drop during 2027. But it believes that the market may see a 6 percent rebound in 2028, as memory supplies improve, pricing begins to stabilize, and pent-up demand for replacement phones returns. The 2026 outlook has been shaped by sharply rising component costs, particularly for DRAM and NAND flash. According to IDC , memory costs have risen approximately 350 percent since last year and are still climbing. As Reg readers will be well aware by now, this has been blamed on the memory manufacturers prioritizing output of high-margin chips to go into AI servers and GPU accelerators, creating a shortage of the mainstream components that are needed for devices like PCs and phones. Vendors have responded by raising prices, reducing memory configurations, and withdrawing lower-cost models. As The Register previously reported , memory costs accounted for almost 60 percent of the total bill of materials in sub-$400 smartphones during Q1 of 2026. For 2027, Counterpoint warns the outlook is for continued tight mobile DRAM supply, further price increases for low-power DDR (LPDDR) memory, and limited evidence to suggest short-term capacity increases. "The 2026 decline was initially expected to mark the low point of the cycle, but the memory situation has remained more restrictive than anticipated," said principal analyst Yang Wang. "Mobile memory allocation is still being displaced by AI and server demand, while higher costs are taking longer to move through handset portfolios and retail channels. The result is a much weaker 2027, particularly for lower priced devices and price sensitive markets." Global shipments are forecast to rebound by 6 percent in 2028, but that would bring shipments only roughly back to this year's already shrunken level, rather than hitting the peak of previous years. Counterpoint cautions that the scale of the rebound will depend on how quickly lower component costs translate into retail pricing. A speedy improvement in mobile memory allocation during the second half of 2027 could bring replacement demand forward and swell shipments, but continued competition from the AI market or another round of handset price increases would hinder recovery. technology.title: Bill for Birmingham's Oracle debacle reaches £128M
technology.description: Birmingham City Council faces a £128.1 million bill for its disastrous transition from SAP to Oracle – more than six times the original estimate for a project that contributed to its financial collapse. Papers presented to its Audit Committee this week put the combined cost of the original implementation, which went live in 2022, and this year's reimplementation at £128.1 million, against £19.96 million forecast in the 2019 business case [PDF]. The report , from program director Philip Macpherson, said the project's funding allocation had previously reached £157 million. The report said the new Oracle Fusion system went live in August without any priority-one or "showstopper" issues. "The program has now moved into the Post Go Live Support phase where [it] continues to provide extra support but slowly transitions towards 'Business As Usual' operating procedures," the report said. It is an understatement to say the same was not true of the first attempt to move the council's finance, HR, and payroll systems off its legacy R/3 SAP system to more modern software. The first project started in 2019 and was supposed to go live in April 2021, but was delayed by a year. After the council started to use the system in April 2022, it soon became beset by a series of serious problems. Although the council had planned to implement Oracle "out-of-the-box," it created several customizations, including a bank reconciliation system that failed to function properly. The council struggled to understand its cash position and was unable to produce auditable accounts . It has spent more than £5 million on manual workaround labor . The system move also contributed to it becoming effectively bankrupt , an event it failed to foresee due to the malfunctioning finance system. It later emerged that officials ignored a "red" warning prior to the go-live date. They were explicitly told the system could cause late payments, a failure to collect debt, and incorrect accounting if it went live. Officials gave the go-ahead regardless. The council decided to reimplement Oracle from scratch, while running the current system as best it could and implementing off-the-shelf software CivicaPay , now rebranded as Civica Income Management. Despite the apparently trouble-free relaunch, the true cost to the council is likely higher than the projected £128.1 million implementation bill. For a start, the original £19 million budget was supposed to support the software implementation for schools , but that was excluded from the reimplementation. Secondly, the council expected significant savings from moving to Oracle in 2022 through greater efficiency. The 2019 business case booked £27 million in savings from 2019 to 2031, for example. A 2024 analysis by Audit Reform Lab, based at the University of Sheffield, estimated that the disaster's direct and indirect financial impact, including lost savings and deteriorating tax collection, would reach £216.5 million by April 2026. technology.title: UK government rejects national consultation on AI datacenters
technology.description: The UK government has rejected calls for a UK-wide public consultation on the environmental impacts of AI datacenters, despite a petition attracting more than 39,000 signatures. Campaign group Protect the Wild launched the petition last month, calling for a national consultation that would consider whether further expansion should be restricted, paused, or halted until those impacts are properly understood and addressed. The nonprofit says the petition smashed the 10,000 signature threshold above which a government response is required in just three days, and the total stood at over 39,000 as this article was being prepared. In its response, published on November 23, the government ruled out the requested UK-wide environmental consultation, saying individual projects' impacts should be addressed through the planning process. It pointed instead to a separate consultation on its draft datacenter planning policy, open until January 8, 2027. "Datacenters are vital to the UK's digital economy. They underpin the digital services that people rely on every day, including public services, healthcare and the way people work. They also provide the infrastructure needed to develop and use AI," the Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST) says. "Building more capacity in the UK will support economic growth and innovation, while strengthening national resilience and ensuring the UK is well placed to realize the opportunities presented by AI." But it adds that the government recognizes the environmental impacts of bit barns are real and must be understood and mitigated, and this is one of the reasons why it established the Data Centre Covenant tests. This Covenant, published last month, sets out tests all compute sheds "are encouraged to meet," while "strategic datacenters" are required to meet them to qualify for additional government assistance. The government has yet to define which datacenters qualify as "strategic," saying it will publish further details and eligibility criteria in due course. Qualifying projects could receive help securing power and accelerating planning. Briefly, the Covenant tests are that operators cover any energy costs they create, so that communities do not have to pick up the bill; that they invest in local communities; adhere to the highest environmental standards; create jobs and drive reindustrialization; and provide secure and reliable access to their compute resources. Reports on Downdetector began rising around 1000 UTC. Lloyds also acknowledged problems on its service status page . A reader who supplied the screenshot below noted the particularly awkward timing: the last Friday of the month is payday for many workers. It's also retail silly season: while Brits don't celebrate Thanksgiving, many UK outlets nonetheless participate in Black Friday sales, meaning storefronts are losing out. Others are concerned with more practical purchases. One customer tweeted that she had "no food at home and cannot shop because I cannot transfer funds from my secondary Lloyds account to my main one. At this point I'm just going to withdraw every penny the moment I'm paid, so much for Internet banking. Never had this years ago." Bank of Scotland, another Lloyds Banking Group brand, reported similar problems on its service status page : " We're aware some customers are having issues with our app and online banking at the moment. We're sorry about this and are working hard to fix it." Earlier this year, a botched overnight software update at Lloyds Banking Group potentially exposed other customers' transaction information to almost 448,000 app users. In a letter to Parliament's Treasury Committee, consumer relationships CEO Jasjyot Singh blamed a defect in the API handling transaction data. The incident affected Lloyds, Halifax, and Bank of Scotland, and prompted goodwill payments to thousands of customers. Lloyds Banking Group said late last year that it had more than 21 million mobile app users and over 23 million digitally active customers. technology.title: Europe's AI sovereignty push: Lots of cloud, not much silver lining
technology.description: Europe's IT spending is growing more slowly than the global average, according to Gartner, whose analysts warn that the region's push for tech sovereignty faces commercial and technological obstacles. Gartner forecasts European IT spending of $1.57 trillion in 2027, up 9.9 percent from 2026, compared with worldwide growth of 15 percent to $7.35 trillion. For 2026, it estimates spending growth of 20.7 percent in North America and 13.7 percent in China. "The world seems to be racing towards this AI goal of where the large language model provider is going to be, and the race seems to be between North American-based providers and some Asia Pacific providers," John-David Lovelock, Distinguished VP Analyst at Gartner, told The Register . He said Europe had traditionally trailed in IT uptake. "We saw that happen when global sourcing, cloud, and software as a service all came along. It's down to the pushback against the idea of creative destruction," where new technologies replace old ones. Europe's fastest growing categories are datacenter systems, forecast to grow 29.7 percent in 2027, and infrastructure as a service, at 26.7 percent. Even so, Lovelock does not expect Europe to compete with North America and China on AI investment. "For AI provision, Europe is going to be behind, and there won't be a way to catch up," he said. "The AI datacenters, the large language models, the foundational models, the tools and techniques for building out AI are all being centered outside of Europe, but enterprises don't need to do that. So the question becomes: regardless of where the source of the AI is coming from, can the enterprises actually adopt and use it? In one sense, Europe will be behind in the provision of AI, but it need not be behind in the use." The gap nonetheless complicates Europe's push to reduce its dependence on US technology suppliers. The European Union has introduced new rules to encourage tech buyers to favor sovereign tech over the dominant tech vendors, but Lovelock doubts they will move spending much. "Sovereignty is a wonderful flag that we fly on the front of a building. IT is running in the basement. CIOs are not going to buy a second-best solution that costs more simply because it's sovereign. "They are not going to break any laws, but they are not going to make a decision that puts their company in a worse position at a higher cost. While sovereignty gets [vendors] on the list, it doesn't assure that they get purchased," he told us. Earlier this month, Gartner predicted that by 2029, more than 90 percent of EU organizations will have a digital sovereignty strategy, but argued that a fully sovereign technology stack remains out of reach. "The global technology supply chain is too interconnected, and many critical dependencies cannot be replaced at a commercially viable scale," said Bettina Tratz-Ryan, VP analyst at Gartner. ®

science.title: Who turned the W upside down? Why Cassiopeia won't sit still
science.description: null Some constellations are like old friends. You know them well, they're always there, and they never seem to change. A case in point is Cassiopeia, the queen. Its beautiful name comes from Greek mythology — the mother of Andromeda — and its shape is said to represent a queen sitting on a throne. To a stargazer, Cassiopeia is best known as a prominent northern constellation shaped like the letter W. It's easy to find — look north, find five reasonably bright stars making a W, congratulate yourself on finding Cassiopeia and use it to get somewhere more interesting. It's so often a signpost, not a destination. But look north a few hours after dark this month, and you'll notice the W has gone. The five stars are still there, but the shape you may have memorized looks like it's been picked up and turned over. It looks more like an E or an M, depending on when you look. Now try and look for the Big Dipper /the Plough. It's gone. Nothing mysterious has happened, of course. Cassiopeia is doing exactly what it always does, but it's a reminder that the northern sky is where you can easily watch the stars move — and the seasons turn. What's happening and when to look Stars move anti-clockwise around the north celestial pole, so Cassiopeia changes orientation. (Image credit: Alan Dyer/Stocktrek Images via Getty Images) Late November is an excellent time to reacquaint yourself with Cassiopeia from anywhere in the Northern Hemisphere. Look high in the northern sky during the evening for its five prominent stars — Caph, Schedar, Navi, Ruchbah and Segin. Depending on exactly when you look, it can look like a W, E, M or a 3. This is because Cassiopeia is circumpolar. Rather than rising in the east and eventually setting in the west like many familiar constellations , it circles the north celestial pole — a position currently held by Polaris , the North Star. From sufficiently northerly latitudes, its main stars never disappear below the horizon. This gives us a simple observing experiment. Find Cassiopeia in the early evening and remember its orientation relative to the horizon. Go back several hours later and look again. The constellation has moved around Polaris, and its shape has changed. The stars haven't changed their arrangement — Earth has simply rotated from west to east. We all know this logically, but watching the familiar pattern of Cassiopeia's stars apparently tip over during a single night makes Earth's rotation a lot less abstract. science.title: On this day in space! Nov. 27, 1885: Astronomer captures 1st known photo of a meteor during an Andromedid meteor storm
science.description: null On Nov. 27, 1885, an astronomer made the first known photograph of a meteor. The picture was taken by Austro-Hungarian astronomer Ladislaus Weinek. He captured the trail of the meteor on a photographic plate in the Czech Republic. The meteor he captured was part of the Andromedid meteor shower . The Andromedids were associated with Biela's Comet , which broke apart in the 1850s. When Weinek observed the meteor shower in 1885, it was in the middle of a meteor storm . This means that there were way more meteors than usual. Skywatchers could see thousands of meteors per hour. The November 1872 incidence of the Andromedid meteor shower, as seen over France, in a painting. (Image credit: Alto Vintage Images/Alamy) Why it mattered Not many stargazers may be be acquainted with the Andromedid meteor shower. What used to be a spectacular annual meteor shower is now hardly even visible. But in 1885, the Andromedids were an annual treat for skywatchers hoping for a chance to see the remains of Biela's comet (a comet first spotted in 1772 and then found - for the third time - in 1826 by the German astronomer Wilhelm von Biela, from whom it gets its name). Meteor Shower Quiz: How Well Do You Know 'Shooting Stars'? This modern photo of the Geminid meteor shower shows dozens of meteors captured in a long exposure by Josh Drury. Ladislaus Weinek, who captured the first photo of a meteor, had to use a photographic plate in 1889. (Image credit: Josh Dury) Camera technology has come a long way since 1885, which is good since it is a bit harder to see the Andromedids these days. Instead of photographic plates or digital cameras, astronomers now have to use special tracking equipment to record images of Andromedid meteors. In 2011, astronomers announced that the meteor shower seemed to be undergoing a resurgence of activity, with 50 meteors per hour, and upticks were expected in 2018 and 2023. Want more space history? These insights could inform the design of plant production systems for future deep-space missions. NASA NASA experiments, including a first-of-its-kind space crop production system, will travel to the International Space Station aboard Northrop Grumman’s 25th Commercial Resupply Services mission for the agency. Investigations from NASA’s Biological and Physical Sciences Division will advance research that benefits life on Earth and future exploration, expanding knowledge of space crops and human health. Groundbreaking space crops Astronauts will need sustainable sources of food to travel farther and stay longer in space. To help understand how crop production works in microgravity, NASA is launching a novel space crops experiment . The new prototype growth chamber will provide critical insights for developing safe, nutritious, and reliable crop production systems for future Moon Base habitats and Mars missions. Knowledge gained from the space crop production system also could help inform agricultural practices such as vertical farming and indoor growing systems. Researchers will use this investigation to validate the system’s water delivery and volume optimization technology aboard the space station. Tiny brain models aboard station A precision health investigation is the next step toward enabling long-duration studies of human brain tissues in space. The research builds on a previous investigation that sent small, lab-grown models of the human brain, called miBrains, to the space station. This experiment will validate a miniature fluid-handling system designed to mix, deliver, and maintain the nutrient-rich liquid needed to keep the tissues alive. Researchers could use the findings to help identify potential neurological risks associated with spaceflight and develop strategies to protect astronaut health. It also may advance human tissue research and neurological disease modeling on Earth. Biological & Physical Sciences Division NASA’s Biological and Physical Sciences Division pioneers scientific discovery and enables exploration by using space environments to conduct investigations not possible on Earth. Studying biological and physical phenomena under extreme conditions allows researchers to advance the fundamental scientific knowledge required to go farther and stay longer in space, while also benefitting life on Earth.

science.title: Astronomers watch a red giant star greedily devour a stellar 'Bao bun' before erupting: 'We couldn't quite believe our luck'
science.description: null Astronomers witnessed the spectacular cosmic indigestion that resulted from a red giant star that devoured a stellar Bao bun in the form of its smaller companion star. That isn't a random comparison. The cannibal star, which is 350 times bigger than the sun, is nicknamed "Big Bao," while its unfortunate companion had the nickname "Little Bao." The cute cosmic monikers come from the fact that this destructive merger event has been designated AT2025abao. A Bao bun might be a little snack for a human, but this red giant star made a real meal out of Little Bao. This cannibalistic event was tracked by a wide array of ground- and space-based telescopes, including NASA space missions NEOWISE, SPHEREx, and the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST), as well as the W. M. Keck Observatory in Hawaii. The conclusion of the event AT2025abao was marked by a massive eruption witnessed in Oct. 2025 by two instruments at Caltech's Palomar Observatory: the Zwicky Transient Facility (ZTF) and the Wide-field INfrared Transient ExploreR (WINTER). "The excitement was real," team member Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University said in a statement sent to Space.com via email. "We couldn't quite believe our luck. With detailed observations for several years before the merger, for the first time, we now have an unprecedented glimpse of the conditions that lead to such cosmic events." Reconstructing a violent cosmic collision The story of AT2025abao began when astronomers detected a bright flash in the nearby Andromeda galaxy , a region where scientists hadn't expected to see a cosmic explosion. Responding to this unexpected flash, Karambelkar and colleagues set about investigating its cause with a plethora of telescopes. This led to them seeing a slow and continuous brightening over the course of two years, They determined the cause of the flash was a rare stellar merger, the luminous red nova now designated AT2025abao. They linked this to a star called WNTR23bzdiq / WTP19aalzlk that had been observed steadily brightening since 2019 after being stable for the preceding 30 years. Thus, the team determined that at the heart of the event is a red giant, a star that puffs out to hundreds of times its original size after it runs out of hydrogen in its core. The team theorizes that Big Bao, with a mass seven times greater than the sun, expanded so rapidly and violently that it swallowed its smaller companion star. The unfortunate star, Little Bao, then spiraled into Big Bao's core in fewer than 10 orbits. "A couple of years back, we discovered a star that was gradually brightening. We took a closer look to discover a red giant, or a star that has started to expand toward the end of its life, just like our sun will one day," Karambelkar said. "Steady brightening was unusual, but even if something was stirring, no one expected to see an explosion in their lifetime, as these stars remain relatively stable for thousands of years." science.title: New Scientist Book Club: How urine changed the course of human history
science.description: A detail from Joseph Wright’s 1771 painting The Alchemist Discovering Phosphorus, showing Henning Brand in 1669 Science History Images/Alamy Imagine you could boil the development of science down to a single ingredient. A magical, mystical compound that transformed human history. Of course, science doesn’t work that way; even if breakthroughs shift the paradigm of our understanding, discovery doesn’t progress like a tech tree in a computer game, but as an interweaving tapestry of complementary and competing ideas and experimentation. Theories can bubble under the surface for centuries, overlooked because of politics or failure to realise their implications, while innovations can emerge from taking an idea in one industry and transplanting it to another. But, for a moment, try and picture what just one such ingredient could be. What would you pick? For centuries, in medieval Europe, alchemists quested for the “Philosopher’s Stone” that would finally help them achieve their dreams of transmutation. It was a search doomed to failure from the very beginning. And yet, a far better idea was under their noses – or, rather, their underpants – the entire time. My pick? Urine has a strong case for being the most transformative substance in human history. Free newsletter Sign up to Book Club Sign up to newsletter The development of civilisation was built on chemistry. It required the first chemical reaction we mastered – fire – to keep us warm, cook our food and smelt ores. But leatherwork played an equally key role. Urine is a source of urea, which bacteria can break down into ammonia, granting early humans easy access to a base that could soften organic matter and tan hides. Across the world, leatherwork became the cornerstone of survival for every civilisation, from the Americas to Europe, Africa and Asia: even cultures that didn’t develop a bronze age, such as the Aztec, or skipped it entirely, as seen in Sub-Saharan Africa, relied on leatherwork for clothes, structures, industry and commerce. Advertisement If the power of pee helped build civilisation, it would go on to be foundational in its upkeep. In ancient Rome, urine was so useful for laundries to keep togas whiter-than-white that Emperor Vespasian levied a tax on draining urinals. When his son complained, Vespasian’s response was blunt: pecunia non olet , money doesn’t stink. Part of the funds were used to build the Colosseum in Rome, today recognised as one of the wonders of the world. The magic of urine filtered into what would become chemical science, too. Cheimeia , the artisanal trade secrets and recipes found in Alexandria, Egypt, that would later give rise to alchemy, recognised the value of urine. In the Leiden Papyrus X , part of a cluster of the only original manuscripts on alchemy’s origins we still have, you can find a recipe for faking gold using polysulfides. Place them in a vessel containing strong vinegar or the urine of a small child. Heat it from below, until the liquid appears like blood. At first, the raider was frustrated; scavenging the tombs near Thebes, he had hoped to uncover a priceless heirloom, or a nugget of gold that would sparkle with lustre in the starlight. Instead, he had found only a clutch of rolled scrolls, made of papyrus and sealed against the elements. For a moment, he considered casting the documents aside and leaving them for the desert. Then greed got the better of him. Westerners loved all things Egyptian, he reasoned. Since the French had arrived with Napoleon, the new field of “Egyptology” had swept the continent, capturing the imagination of scholars and the wealthy. It was almost as popular as the new science of “chemistry”. Surely, if he took his find to the market, he’d find some gullible fool willing to buy it. The buyer’s name was Jean d’Anastasy, and he was anything but a fool. Born in Greece as the son of a Damascus merchant who had won and lost his fortune in the Napoleonic Wars, d’Anastasy had used his family’s connections to set himself up as a grain merchant in Alexandria, before scheming his way into being named the local Consul General for Sweden and Norway. He quickly saw the value of the papers, paid for them, and shipped them back to Europe. Some went to Stockholm, and some to Leiden University in the Netherlands. When the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 captured this image on November 8, 2026, clouds encroached on the snowy mountain on Russia’s Kamchatka Peninsula . But they hovered beneath the volcano’s 3,283-meter (10,771-foot) peak, leaving a clear opening over its caldera and northern upper slopes. The upper reaches of Shivelyuch feature a caldera 9 kilometers (5.6 miles) wide that is open to the south. A lava dome , formed by vents extruding viscous magma, appears as a dark area within it. Lava domes on Shivelyuch go through cycles of growth and collapse, with collapses sometimes setting off fast-moving avalanches of hot ash and rock called pyroclastic flows . In November 2026, effusive eruptions of lava and explosive activity at Shivelyuch had been ongoing for months , according to reports from the Kamchatka Volcanic Eruption Response Team (KVERT). And despite frequent cloudiness, satellites regularly detect thermal anomalies from the volcano. On the day of this image, KVERT reported that a plume of resuspended ash drifted 120 kilometers (75 miles) to the east. That kind of activity is relatively tame for the mountain. Explosions from Shivelyuch periodically send ash several kilometers up into the atmosphere, where it can travel great distances and pose risks to aircraft . In July 2026, an ash plume rode the jet stream over the Bering Sea into Alaskan airspace, according to news reports , prompting the cancellation of multiple flights. science.description:
Richard's love affair with outer space started when he saw the original "Star Wars" on TV aged four, and he spent much of the ’90s watching "Star Trek”, "Babylon 5” and “The X-Files" with his mum. After studying physics at university, he became a journalist, swapped science fact for science fiction, and hit the jackpot when he joined the team at SFX, the UK's biggest sci-fi and fantasy magazine. He liked it so much he stayed there for 12 years, four of them as editor. 

He's since gone freelance and passes his time writing about "Star Wars", "Star Trek" and superheroes for the likes of SFX, Total Film, TechRadar and GamesRadar+. He has met five Doctors, two Starfleet captains and one Luke Skywalker, and once sat in the cockpit of "Red Dwarf"'s Starbug.  

It may have been subtitled "The Voyage Home", but to most viewers "Star Trek IV" (which has just turned 40) will always be "the one with the whales". After "The Wrath of Khan" and "The Search for Spock" went to some pretty dark places — ear worms, the destruction of the Enterprise, the death (and later resurrection) of a certain beloved Vulcan — the franchise was in need of some light relief. So what better than to set coordinates for the then-present day of 1986 San Francisco, for a time-travel comedy romp? Spock himself, Leonard Nimoy, had directed "The Search for Spock" and Paramount had lined him up to call the shots on a follow-up before the movie had even landed in theaters. They gave him freedom to tell the story he wanted to tell, and he landed on a not obviously box-office-friendly formula of "No dying, no fighting, no shooting, no photon torpedoes, no phaser blasts, no stereotypical bad guy". It was a massive shift away from Khan and Kruge, the grandstanding villains in movies II and III. Nimoy also wanted the film to have an environmental message and appeal beyond the franchise's traditional fanbase. The film would actually be promoted with minimal "Trek" branding in some territories. (Image credit: Paramount) "I wanted to make it accessible to people who don't go to 'Star Trek' movies," Nimoy said in "The Fifty-Year Mission" by Edward Gross and Mark A. Altman. "The Voyage Home" effectively closes the trilogy that began four years earlier with "The Wrath of Khan". science.title: Venus shines at its brightest in the predawn sky this week. Here's where to look
science.description: null Venus is at its most dazzling in the predawn sky this week as it shines close to the bright star Spica in the southeast. Here's what you need to know. As an inner planet, Venus never strays far from the horizon, at least compared to outer planets like Jupiter and Mars which can be visible all night long during opposition, when they shine opposite the sun in Earth's sky. Instead, Venus alternates between morning and evening appearances. All the while, its shifting moon-like phases and ever-changing proximity to Earth causes its brightness to wax and wane. When is Venus at its most dazzling? Venus will reach peak brightness during its current morning apparition at 1:37 p.m. EST (1837 GMT) on Nov. 27 according to the astronomy website In-The-Sky . Stargazers in the U.S. could get an incredible view of Venus in the predawn hours of the coming week, as the planet climbs into the southeastern sky ahead of the rising sun, with Mercury clinging close to the horizon below. Celestron Nexstar 4SE (Image credit: Celestron) This is a fantastic go-to telescope with a 4-inch aperture and can help you quickly find a steady view of the moon. For a closer look at craters and the terminator, make sure to grab a 9mm or 12mm eyepiece and get stronger magnification. _ Celestron Nexstar 4SE review The bright star Spica will glow less than five degrees away from Venus before dawn on Nov. 27 — roughly the width of your three middle fingers held at arm's length against the night sky. Spica is a double system of two stars that orbit one another once every four days. Its stars are separated by just approximately 11 million miles (less than 18 million kilometers), making them far too close to split visually with even the most powerful amateur equipment. However, the system still makes for a dazzling target, appearing as a magnificent blue-white star when viewed through the eyepiece of a 4-inch telescope. Venus will appear close to Spica in the southeastern sky. (Image credit: Starry Night Pro 8) Check that the sun is safely below the horizon before turning your telescope on Venus to observe a crescent of light playing across the planet's dense atmosphere. Over the coming weeks and months, Venus will appear increasingly illuminated as it moves farther away from Earth in its orbit, while its apparent size through a telescope will gradually decrease. science.title: On this day in space! Nov. 26, 2011: NASA's 2-ton nuclear-powered Curiosity rover launches to Mars
science.description: null On November 26, 2011, the NASA Curiosity rover launched to Mars. The Mars rover Curiosity was the biggest and most powerful rover anyone had ever sent to the Red Planet. The 2-ton science laboratory is about the size of a small SUV. The mission's goal was to search for habitable environments on Mars , or evidence that the planet could have been habitable in the past. It launched on an Atlas V rocket from Cape Canaveral Air Force Station in Florida. About nine months later, Curiosity made a challenging landing on Mars. It successfully used a new landing technology called a sky crane to gently lower it to the surface. NASA's Curiosity rover lifts off atop a United Launch Alliance Atlas V rocket on Nov. 26, 2011 from Florida's Cape Canaveral Air Force Station. (Image credit: collectSPACE/Robert Z. Pearlman ) Why it mattered It may be hard to imagine now, but 15 years ago, the idea of a nuclear-powered rover on Mars was just a concept. When the Curiosity rover launched in 2011, it made that idea a reality the car-size probe (using a plutonium-based radioisotope thermoelectric generator that converts heat from radioactive decay into power) as it headed to the Red Planet. Curiosity was the largest rover ever launched to Mars, following up on the success of the tiny Sojourner rover in 1997 and the larger twin rovers Spirit and Opportunity in 2004. Its sky crane landing system was novel at the time, and fully automated. Once it began its descent in August 2012, NASA could only wait through "seven minutes of terror" to see how it turned out. It ended being a huge success. NASA's Curiosity rover on Mars. (Image credit: NASA) After its smooth landing, Curiosity lived up to its original name: the Mars Science Laboratory. Within weeks, Curiosity fulfilled its primary mission. It found evidence of ancient running water on Mars . It later found organic molecules on Mars as well. Curiosity's primary mission was expected to last just about one Martian year (687 Earth days, or about two Earth years), as the rover explored its Gale Crater landing site. But NASA has extended the mission as the rover continues to operate in good health. In fact, Curiosity has survived long enough to welcome its successor to Mars, the Perseverance rover , which landed in February 2021 on a mission to collect the first samples for later retrieval. Perseverance used the same basic 2-ton design, plutonium power system and sky crane landing system to reach Mars. And today, a ground-based twin of the Curiosity rover, called Promise , is being outfitted for an upcoming mission to the moon. Want more space history? science.title: Rocket Lab launches Japanese satellite into orbit in record-setting Thanksgiving Day liftoff (video)
science.description: null Rocket Lab added another satellite to a growing Japanese Earth-observation constellation on Thanksgiving Day (Nov. 26) in a record-setting liftoff for the company. An Electron rocket carrying a radar imaging satellite for Tokyo-based Earth-observation company Synspective is scheduled to lift off from Rocket Lab 's New Zealand launch site Thursday, during a window that opened 7 p.m. ET (0000 GMT/1 p.m. on Nov. 27 in New Zealand). It was the 22nd launch of the year for Rocket Lab, a new high record. "We set the pace, and then we break our own records," Rocket Lab said in an update on social media . It was the 101st launch overall for the company. You can see the mission, called "Night Owls Never Sleep," via Rocket Lab in the YouTube video at the top of this page. A Rocket Lab Electron rocket launches the Japanese radar satellite for the company Synspective's Strix imaging constellation on Nov. 26, 2026. (Image credit: Rocket Lab) We set the pace, and then we break our own records. "Night Owls Never Sleep" was our 22nd launch of the year - a new annual launch record for Electron. https://t.co/pzckdctiOE November 27, 2026 Synspective is building a network of "Strix" spacecraft equipped with synthetic aperture radar (SAR), which uses radio waves to generate detailed images of Earth's surface in both day and night lighting, as well as through cloud cover. Thursday's launch will be Rocket Lab's 14th for Synspective to date, and there are a lot more coming. At the end of September, Rocket Lab announced a deal with the company for an additional 20 Electron missions between 2028 and 2031 — the largest commercial launch contract in the rocket's history. That agreement brought Synspective's total number of contracted Electron flights to 47. Synspective aims to eventually establish a constellation capable of imaging locations anywhere on Earth at intervals of just a few hours. After its successful launch, the Electron's kick stage deployed the Strix satellite into low Earth orbit , 569 kilometers (353.6 miles) above our planet. "Night Owl Never Sleeps" marked the 101st mission to date for Rocket Lab. Ninety-two of them have been orbital flights with Electron; the other nine have been missions with HASTE , a suborbital variant of Electron that allows customers to test sensors and other equipment in the hypersonic flight environment. Editor's note: This story was updated on Nov. 27, 2026 to reflect the successful launch of Rocket Lab's Electron rocket for Synspective.
